synopsis: Komatsu provides a precedent for restricted-domain releases rather than broad site coverage: documented interventions were limited by direction, speed, model or trigger, and KomVision began on Japan’s PC200-11 excavator, going on sale in December 2019 before its 30 March 2020 announcement [f11166, f10897, f10633]. KomVision detects people with cameras and stops excavators when travel or swing starts, but not during an ongoing swing; Komatsu also requires disabling excavator stop control during trailer loading because rapid stops can destabilize the machine, while wheel-loader cautions extend to slopes, slippery or soft ground and suspended loads [f11425, f11426, f11427, f10550]. Wabtec’s December 2021 Level 9 validation covered Komatsu 730E and 860E trucks at up to 30 km/h and still used physical tests to adjust detection zones; the booklet found neither independent performance tests nor published validation methods, durations or physical-testing shares for the cited Komatsu products [f817, f1247, f1242, f1389]. The multi-year Applied Intuition–Komatsu partnership announced on 9 September 2025 covers Vehicle OS, autonomous haulage and collision avoidance for staffed sites, including planned EMESRT control level 9 development; Applied Intuition is both a tool and autonomy-stack supplier, but its productivity case studies are not controlled cross-vendor measurements [f8399, f8400, f8332, f8735]. Komatsu also describes terrain-and-environment digital twins, while a 2024 wheel-loader digging model co-funded by Komatsu and Algoryx required a tire-ground friction coefficient of 2.0 to match measurements, highlighting a concrete simulation-calibration issue [f4125, f6090].
